The abbreviation B.C.E. (Before Common Era) and negative years are general conventions used to represent eras that precede the earliest recorded dates in our calendars.

Prerequisites

The study of genealogy draws on several subjects: mathematics, literature, the languages in which the documents are written, history, and biology. We know that not everyone has time to study all of them in depth. To help you, we have gathered the following texts, which will serve as a foundation for studying genealogy:

  • Origin: a general overview of the origin of our species, based both on scientific research and on various beliefs ().
  • Scientific method: an explanation of the scientific method, including an example you can try at home ().
  • Understanding Texts: a section that teaches techniques for understanding texts and explores the relationship between those texts and mathematics ().
  • My Ancestors: a guide to help you obtain the necessary documentation and begin building your family tree ().
  • Sources: an explanation of the various sources used in research ().
  • Natural Limits: an introduction to the concept of limits, using examples from the human body and from liquids ().
  • Chronology: an introduction to the various archaeological periods currently in use ().
  • Genealogical Trees (Chapter 1): studying families only when documents are available makes it harder to understand who we are and leads to many misunderstandings, such as reading poetic texts as if they were literal descriptions of reality ().

We therefore recommend studying the first chapter of the Genealogical Trees section before continuing with the remaining chapters.

Some families may need extra information. When that happens, the additional details will be listed below.

Navigation

The family tree page of History Tracers is organized into three main sections:

  • Patriarch/Matriarch list: a list of the patriarchs and matriarchs who named a family or lived in a particular region.
  • People grouped by family: when you click a family name or a region in the first section, you are taken to a page that introduces the first documented person, together with their descendants and a brief account of their lives. Texts supported by primary sources appear in normal font, while hypotheses without verifiable sources appear in italics. Each account is accompanied by its primary sources and references, which you can open with a single click.
  • Primary sources and references: a common mistake among genealogy researchers is to assume that the author of a book followed the scientific method rigorously when writing about their own family history, and that the book needs no further checking. To avoid this misleading assumption, the page clearly separates primary sources, which confirm beyond doubt that a person existed, from other references, such as those found in noble genealogies. Religious texts are placed in a separate, respectful section; however, if such a text was written during the lifetime of the people it mentions, it can also be cited as a primary source.
